Chapter 7: Redefining Success—Letting Go of Old Measures
You know, for most of us, success always seems just out of reach. When we’re young, it’s all about grades, trophies, promotions, maybe even a little applause. But then something happens—illness enters the picture, and suddenly, those old yardsticks just don’t fit anymore. The world’s definition of achievement—fame, wealth, recognition—can start to feel pretty hollow, maybe even a little cruel, when your body just won’t cooperate.
Imagine this: there’s a memory of a parent, someone who used to be the breadwinner, the life of every party. Now, they’re struggling just to tie their own shoes. The frustration is real, and the sense of loss? Overwhelming. But then, their child steps in to help. And in that moment, something shifts. Accepting that help, letting yourself be vulnerable—suddenly, that becomes a new kind of success. It’s not about what you can accomplish alone anymore, but about what you’re willing to share, and receive.
For so many people, living with illness is really about letting go—letting go of old dreams, old identities, and the old ways we measure our worth. It’s about finding value right here, in the present moment. It’s in your relationships, in small acts of kindness, in gentle moments. Think about it—a walk around the block, a home-cooked meal, a good, honest conversation. These become your new milestones. And you know what? That’s worth celebrating.
Even work starts to look different. That old drive to be the best, to chase achievements, slowly gets replaced by a desire for something deeper—purpose, and real connection. Maybe you find fulfillment in mentoring someone, or sharing your story. Or maybe you throw yourself into causes that really matter to you. Some folks even discover hidden talents—painting, writing, gardening—that bring a whole new kind of joy.
Of course, redefining success isn’t easy. It takes humility, patience, and a willingness to see yourself in a whole new way. There are definitely moments of grief for what you’ve lost, but there are also moments of gratitude for what you still have. And bit by bit, it becomes clearer—success isn’t about what you own, or what you achieve. It’s about who you are, and how you love.
Now, the world might not always get this new definition. Some people might judge, or pity, or just not see the quiet courage it takes to keep going. But if you’ve ever walked this path, you know the truth: real success isn’t measured in accolades. It’s found in resilience, in compassion, and in the ability to find meaning—even when things get tough.
